metadata.analysis_scope: Ethereum Execution Layer (Geth) - analyzing all actors, components, and trust boundaries in operational scenarios

actors.name: Consensus Client (CL)
actors.description: Paired beacon chain client (e.g., Prysm, Lighthouse, Teku, Nimbus) that communicates with Geth via authenticated Engine API to coordinate block production and fork choice

operational_scenarios.description: Protocol team or single validator operator runs both Geth and paired CL on same infrastructure
trust_implications: Assumed honest operation of both EL and CL by same operator
Local authenticated connection reduces MITM risk
Single point of failure: compromise of infrastructure affects both layers
operational_scenarios.deployment_pattern: Common for solo validators and protocol testing

operational_scenarios.description: Institutional staking provider runs Geth paired with CL operated by known partner (e.g., white-label staking services)
trust_implications: Trust that CL operator provides honest fork choice updates
Network authentication (JWT) critical to prevent unauthorized Engine API access
Split responsibility: EL operator trusts CL for liveness, not for safety (EL validates all payloads)
operational_scenarios.deployment_pattern: Used by institutional staking providers with separate teams

operational_scenarios.description: User accidentally connects Geth to wrong network's CL or malicious CL instance
trust_implications: Malicious CL can DoS Geth with invalid payloads, triggering repeated validation failures
Malicious CL can withhold block proposals, preventing validator from earning rewards
EL CANNOT be forced to accept invalid state (all payloads validated against consensus rules)
Worst case: liveness failure, NOT safety failure
operational_scenarios.deployment_pattern: Edge case: user error or social engineering attack

actors.trust_level_rationale: Trusted for LIVENESS (providing payloads, fork choice updates) but NOT for SAFETY. Geth validates all received payloads and will reject invalid blocks even from paired CL.
capabilities_if_honest: Provides canonical fork choice view (headBlockHash, safeBlockHash, finalizedBlockHash)
Requests block building with valid payload attributes (timestamp, feeRecipient, withdrawals, beaconRoot)
Submits network-received blocks for validation via engine_newPayload
Triggers chain reorganizations via engine_forkchoiceUpdated
capabilities_if_malicious: DoS Geth by sending invalid payloads repeatedly (triggers validation overhead)
Request building blocks with invalid attributes (rejected by Geth)
Withhold fork choice updates causing Geth to fall behind canonical chain
Request reorgs to non-existent or invalid blocks (Geth enters SYNCING state)
CANNOT force Geth to accept invalid state root, transactions, or consensus rule violations
mitigations: All Engine API methods authenticated via JWT (--authrpc.jwtsecret)
Engine API exposed only on localhost by default (--authrpc.addr)
Geth fully validates all received payloads against consensus rules
Invalid blocks tracked ephemerally with hit-count eviction (never persisted)
Geth monitors CL liveness and warns if no updates received for 2 minutes

actors.name: Node Operator
actors.description: Individual or organization running Geth node with control over configuration, keystore, RPC exposure, and system resources

operational_scenarios.description: Individual runs Geth on home hardware with local keystore for validator signing
trust_implications: Full control over private keys, configuration, and RPC exposure
Responsible for securing keystore passphrase and file permissions
Vulnerable to local system compromise (malware, physical access)
Must correctly configure fork activation parameters (--override.osaka, etc.)
operational_scenarios.deployment_pattern: Common in decentralized validator set

operational_scenarios.description: Staking service or exchange runs Geth fleet with centralized key management
trust_implications: Uses external signer (Clef) or HSM for key isolation
RPC endpoints may be exposed to internal services (monitoring, trading bots)
Configuration drift risk across fleet
Insider threat: operators have god-mode access to signing keys
operational_scenarios.deployment_pattern: Used by Coinbase, Kraken, Lido node operators

operational_scenarios.description: Operator exposes dangerous RPC endpoints publicly or uses weak keystore passwords
trust_implications: Exposed --http.api=admin,debug allows remote code execution (debug_setHead, admin_startRPC)
Exposed personal namespace (deprecated) allows account unlocking
Weak keystore password enables key theft via brute force
Incorrect fork configuration causes chain split from network
operational_scenarios.deployment_pattern: Security anti-pattern, unfortunately common (bots scan for open RPC)

actors.trust_level_rationale: Node operator has ultimate control over Geth instance and is inherently trusted. Compromise of operator = compromise of node.
capabilities_if_honest: Configure fork activation parameters to match network consensus
Manage private keys securely in keystore with strong passphrases
Expose RPC endpoints only to trusted local/internal services
Monitor node health and respond to liveness issues
Upgrade Geth to patch vulnerabilities
capabilities_if_malicious: Expose dangerous RPC namespaces (admin, debug, personal) to internet
Use weak keystore passwords enabling brute force attacks
Configure incorrect fork activation blocks causing consensus split
Extract private keys from keystore for theft or unauthorized signing
Manipulate local state database (though this causes peer rejection)
Deploy backdoored Geth binary with embedded key exfiltration
mitigations: Geth defaults to safe RPC configuration: only eth, net, web3 namespaces on HTTP
Admin/debug namespaces require explicit --http.api flag (warning issued)
Account unlocking forbidden over HTTP/WebSocket by default
Keystore files encrypted with scrypt KDF (configurable work factor)
Documentation warns about RPC exposure risks
Clef (external signer) isolates key management from node operation

actors.name: P2P Network Peers
actors.description: Ethereum execution layer peer-to-peer network participants exchanging blocks, transactions, and protocol messages via ETH/68 and ETH/69 protocols

operational_scenarios.description: Majority of peers run honest Geth/Besu/Nethermind implementations following consensus rules
trust_implications: Geth can sync chain state from any honest peer
Transaction propagation ensures mempool diversity
Block propagation enables timely fork choice awareness
Peer diversity reduces censorship risk
operational_scenarios.deployment_pattern: Normal operation on Ethereum mainnet

operational_scenarios.description: Attacker controls all peer connections to victim Geth node, isolating it from honest network
trust_implications: Victim receives only attacker's blocks and transactions
Attacker can censor specific transactions from victim's view
Attacker can delay block propagation to cause sync lag
Victim consensus client will detect finality mismatch if eclipse lasts >2 epochs
operational_scenarios.deployment_pattern: Advanced network attack requiring IP-level manipulation

operational_scenarios.description: Attacker spawns many malicious peers to flood victim with invalid blocks/txs
trust_implications: Geth spends CPU validating invalid messages before rejection
Bandwidth exhaustion if attacker sends max-size messages (10MB)
Peer reputation system eventually blacklists malicious peers
Node remains safe (invalid messages rejected) but liveness impacted
operational_scenarios.deployment_pattern: DoS attack vector, mitigated by peer scoring

actors.trust_level_rationale: P2P peers assumed adversarial. Geth validates ALL received data before state incorporation. Peers can impact liveness (DoS) but not safety.
capabilities_if_honest: Propagate valid blocks to peers via NewBlockMsg
Propagate valid transactions via TransactionsMsg or NewPooledTransactionHashesMsg
Respond to GetBlockHeaders, GetBlockBodies, GetReceipts requests
Respond to GetPooledTransactions for announced transaction hashes
Provide recent chain state for snap sync
capabilities_if_malicious: Send invalid blocks causing validation overhead (rejected after ValidateBody/ValidateState)
Send oversized messages up to 10MB protocol limit to waste bandwidth
Withhold announced transactions (tx hash advertised but GetPooledTransactions fails)
Send equivocating messages (different blocks to different peers)
Exhaust peer connection slots via Sybil attack
CANNOT force acceptance of invalid state, transactions, or consensus violations
mitigations: All received blocks validated via BlockValidator.ValidateBody and ValidateState
All received transactions validated via TxPool validation (signature, nonce, balance, gas)
Message size limit enforced (10MB max per ETH protocol)
Peer reputation tracking: misbehaving peers blacklisted
Fork ID validation prevents cross-network pollution
MaxPeers limit (default 50) prevents connection exhaustion
Inbound connection throttling (30s per source IP)

actors.name: Transaction Submitter (User/Wallet/DApp)
actors.description: External entity submitting signed transactions to Geth mempool via eth_sendRawTransaction RPC or P2P propagation

operational_scenarios.description: End user submits transaction via MetaMask/Rabby/hardware wallet to public/private RPC endpoint
trust_implications: User's wallet signs transaction locally (Geth never sees private key)
RPC provider (if third-party) can censor transaction by not relaying it
Malicious RPC can return fake transaction hash without broadcasting
Transaction validation ensures user cannot submit invalid tx (insufficient balance, bad nonce, etc.)
operational_scenarios.deployment_pattern: Standard user interaction with Ethereum

operational_scenarios.description: MEV bot submits bundle to Flashbots/private mempool or direct to validator
trust_implications: Searcher may use private RPC to avoid front-running by public mempool
Validator operator (running Geth) sees transaction before inclusion
No additional trust: transaction still validated via standard rules
Censorship possible if validator colludes with specific searchers
operational_scenarios.deployment_pattern: MEV supply chain, ~90% of Ethereum blocks

operational_scenarios.description: Attacker submits flood of transactions to DoS mempool or waste block space
trust_implications: Each transaction must pay gas, limiting economic viability of spam
TxPool has size limits (default 4096 pending, 1024 queued per account)
Low gas price transactions evicted when pool full
Block builders prioritize by effective priority fee, naturally filtering spam
operational_scenarios.deployment_pattern: DoS attempt, economically deterred by gas fees

actors.trust_level_rationale: Transaction submitters assumed adversarial. Geth validates signature, nonce, balance, gas before mempool admission. Invalid transactions rejected.
capabilities_if_honest: Submit valid signed transaction with correct nonce, sufficient balance, adequate gas
Pay appropriate gas fees for desired inclusion speed
Use EIP-1559 dynamic fees (type 0x02) for fee market efficiency
Submit blob transactions (type 0x03) for L2 data availability
capabilities_if_malicious: Submit transaction with invalid signature (rejected: signature verification fails)
Submit transaction with insufficient balance (rejected: balance check fails)
Submit transaction with replay attack signature (rejected: chainID mismatch or nonce duplicate)
Spam mempool with low-fee transactions (evicted by fee market)
Submit blob transaction with invalid KZG commitment (rejected: proof verification fails)
CANNOT bypass validation: all transactions must pass ValidateTransaction checks
mitigations: Signature verification via ECDSA secp256k1 recovers sender address
EIP-155 replay protection via chainID in signature
Nonce check prevents duplicate transaction inclusion
Balance check ensures sender can pay gas + value
Gas limit check prevents under-gassed transactions
Blob transaction KZG proof verification ensures data availability
TxPool size limits prevent memory exhaustion
Fee market naturally filters spam via economic cost

actors.name: RPC Client (DApp Backend/Indexer/User)
actors.description: External service or user querying Geth state via JSON-RPC (eth_call, eth_getBalance, eth_getLogs, etc.) over HTTP/WebSocket/IPC

operational_scenarios.description: Infura/Alchemy/Ankr provides public RPC endpoint with rate limits and read-only access
trust_implications: Clients trust RPC provider to return accurate state data
Malicious RPC can return fake balances, logs, call results
Clients should verify critical data via multiple providers or light client
RPC provider cannot modify chain state (read-only access)
operational_scenarios.deployment_pattern: Standard DApp backend relying on third-party RPC

operational_scenarios.description: Organization runs private Geth with authenticated RPC for internal services (trading, monitoring)
trust_implications: Internal services trust RPC provider (same organization)
Authentication prevents unauthorized access but not malicious insider
If admin/debug namespaces enabled, RPC client has god-mode access
Critical: never expose admin/debug to untrusted clients
operational_scenarios.deployment_pattern: Enterprise staking infrastructure

operational_scenarios.description: Attacker with RPC access attempts to exploit node via crafted requests
trust_implications: Read-only namespaces (eth, net, web3) cannot modify state
Admin namespace (if exposed) allows arbitrary peer manipulation, RPC config changes
Debug namespace allows trace replay with arbitrary gas limits (potential DoS)
Personal namespace (deprecated) allowed account unlocking over network
operational_scenarios.deployment_pattern: Attack vector if dangerous namespaces exposed

actors.trust_level_rationale: RPC clients assumed adversarial. Default configuration exposes only read-only namespaces. Admin/debug require explicit operator configuration.
capabilities_if_honest: Query chain state: balances, storage, code, logs, receipts
Simulate transactions via eth_call (no state change)
Subscribe to new block headers, logs, pending transactions (WebSocket)
Retrieve historical data within configured retention period
capabilities_if_malicious: DoS via expensive queries (eth_getLogs with wide block range) - mitigated by RPCGlobalLogQueryLimit
DoS via eth_call with excessive gas - mitigated by RPCGlobalGasCapFlag
If admin exposed: manipulate peer connections (admin_addPeer, admin_removePeer)
If debug exposed: trigger expensive trace operations (debug_traceBlock)
If personal exposed (deprecated): attempt account unlocking
CANNOT modify chain state via read-only namespaces
mitigations: Default HTTP API whitelist: only eth, net, web3 (safe read-only namespaces)
Admin/debug require explicit --http.api flag with documentation warnings
Personal namespace deprecated and removed
RPCGlobalGasCapFlag limits eth_call gas (default 50M gas)
RPCGlobalLogQueryLimit caps eth_getLogs results (default 10000 logs)
RPCGlobalEVMTimeoutFlag limits execution time (default 5s)
Batch request limits prevent amplification attacks

actors.name: Clef (External Signer)
actors.description: Standalone transaction signing daemon that manages keystores and provides signing services to Geth or other clients, isolating key material from node operation

operational_scenarios.description: Clef runs on USB Armory or dedicated hardware, signs transactions via IPC for paired Geth
trust_implications: Key material isolated from internet-connected Geth node
Requires physical access to USB device for signing approval
Compromised Geth cannot extract keys (stored in Clef, not Geth)
User must manually approve each transaction via Clef UI
operational_scenarios.deployment_pattern: High-security validator setup, similar to hardware wallet

operational_scenarios.description: Clef runs with automated rule engine for MEV bot or trading system
trust_implications: Rules allow automatic signing without manual approval (convenience vs security tradeoff)
Compromised Geth could trick Clef into signing malicious transactions if rules too permissive
Rate limiting in rules mitigates theft but doesn't prevent it entirely
Audit log tracks all signing requests for forensics
operational_scenarios.deployment_pattern: Institutional staking with automated operations

operational_scenarios.description: Attacker gains access to Clef binary or its encrypted master seed
trust_implications: Master seed encrypted with user passphrase (scrypt KDF)
Weak passphrase enables key extraction
Clef audit log may reveal attacker activity
Equivalent to compromising Geth keystore if Clef accessible
operational_scenarios.deployment_pattern: Security failure scenario

actors.trust_level_rationale: Clef trusted for key custody and signing decisions. Compromise of Clef = compromise of keys. Used to REDUCE attack surface by isolating keys from Geth.
capabilities_if_honest: Store and manage encrypted keystores with scrypt KDF
Sign transactions after user approval or rule-based authorization
Provide UI for transaction review (shows decoded call data, warnings)
Maintain audit log of all signing requests and approvals
Support hardware wallets (Ledger, Trezor) as signing backends
capabilities_if_malicious: Sign arbitrary transactions without user knowledge (if rules misconfigured)
Exfiltrate private keys to attacker (if Clef binary backdoored)
Approve phishing transactions if user tricked by malicious DApp
Rate limit bypass if rules not properly restrictive
mitigations: Clef External API (untrusted): does not accept credentials or assume authority
User approval required for each transaction unless explicit rules configured
Keystore encrypted with scrypt (configurable work factor)
Audit log tracks all signing activity
4byte database identifies known method selectors for user review
Warning issued for suspicious transactions (invalid checksum, unusual data)

actors.name: Block Builder / MEV Relay
actors.description: OPTIONAL external service that constructs blocks for validators via MEV-Boost, optimizing transaction ordering for maximal extractable value

operational_scenarios.description: Validator operator connects Geth to Flashbots/BloXroute relay for outsourced block building
trust_implications: Relay builds block with private order flow, validator blindly signs header
Validator trusts relay to include valid transactions and pay promised fee
Relay CANNOT include invalid transactions (validator's Geth validates payload post-signing)
Censorship risk: relay may exclude certain transactions (e.g., Tornado Cash)
Liveness dependency: if relay offline, validator cannot propose
operational_scenarios.deployment_pattern: ~90% of Ethereum validators use MEV-Boost as of 2024

operational_scenarios.description: Validator builds blocks locally using Geth's built-in miner (no external relay)
trust_implications: Full control over transaction selection and ordering
No censorship risk from external party
Lower MEV revenue (no access to private order flow)
Simpler security model: no external dependency
operational_scenarios.deployment_pattern: Solo validators prioritizing censorship resistance

operational_scenarios.description: Relay builds invalid block or withholds block after validator signs header
trust_implications: If block invalid: validator's Geth rejects payload via engine_newPayload, attestation missed
If block withheld: network doesn't receive block, slot missed, validator penalized
Relay CANNOT steal validator keys or force signing of invalid state root
Worst case: liveness failure (missed attestations), not slashing
operational_scenarios.deployment_pattern: Attack vector or relay infrastructure failure

actors.trust_level_rationale: Trusted for LIVENESS and MEV REVENUE, not for SAFETY. Geth validates all received payloads. Relay can cause missed slots but cannot force acceptance of invalid state.
capabilities_if_honest: Build blocks with optimized transaction ordering for maximal MEV revenue
Include private order flow from searchers not visible in public mempool
Provide block to validator before proposal deadline
Pay validator promised block value in coinbase or separate payment
capabilities_if_malicious: Withhold block after validator signs header (causes missed slot)
Build block with excluded transactions (censorship)
Pay less than promised block value (theft, but detectable)
Include invalid transactions (rejected by validator's Geth during engine_newPayload)
CANNOT force validator to accept invalid state root or consensus violations
mitigations: Validator's Geth validates all received payloads via engine_newPayload
Block validation occurs AFTER header signed but BEFORE attestation
Relay reputation system: validators switch to honest relays if misbehavior detected
Min-bid configuration allows validator to reject low-value blocks
Local fallback: validator can build block locally if relay fails
source_of_truth: https://github.com/flashbots/mev-boost (external dependency, not in Geth codebase)
actors.note: MEV-Boost is NOT part of Geth codebase. It's an external middleware that sits between CL and Geth. Included in trust model because it's operationally critical for >90% of validators.

actors.name: Node Deployer / DevOps
actors.description: Individual or team responsible for deploying Geth binary, configuring startup flags, and managing infrastructure (distinct from ongoing node operator)

operational_scenarios.description: DevOps downloads Geth from official GitHub releases, verifies GPG signature, deploys to production
trust_implications: Trust that ethereum/go-ethereum repository not compromised
Trust that GPG signing key not stolen
Trust that build reproducibility matches published checksums
Correct initial configuration critical (fork params, bootnodes, JWT secret)
operational_scenarios.deployment_pattern: Best practice deployment

operational_scenarios.description: Attacker compromises GitHub release, build pipeline, or distribution channel to inject backdoored Geth binary
trust_implications: Backdoored binary could exfiltrate keys, manipulate RPC responses, or cause consensus failures
GPG signature verification only helps if signing key not compromised
Reproducible builds allow independent verification but rarely performed
Docker image from Docker Hub could be malicious (not signed)
operational_scenarios.deployment_pattern: Advanced persistent threat (APT) scenario

operational_scenarios.description: DevOps uses wrong network config, exposes dangerous RPC namespaces, or disables critical features
trust_implications: Wrong --networkid or --bootnodes connects to wrong chain (testnet vs mainnet)
Exposed --http.api=admin,debug,personal allows remote exploitation
Missing --authrpc.jwtsecret allows unauthorized Engine API access
Disabled --snapshot or wrong --syncmode causes slow sync or excessive disk usage
operational_scenarios.deployment_pattern: Configuration error, unfortunately common

actors.trust_level_rationale: Deployer has root-level control over Geth binary and configuration. Compromise at deployment = compromise of node from inception.
capabilities_if_honest: Download Geth from official sources and verify GPG signatures
Configure fork activation parameters correctly (--override.osaka, etc.)
Generate secure JWT secret for Engine API authentication
Set safe RPC API exposure (default or --http.api=eth,net,web3)
Deploy on hardened infrastructure with proper firewall rules
capabilities_if_malicious: Deploy backdoored Geth binary with embedded key exfiltration
Configure incorrect fork parameters causing chain split
Expose dangerous RPC namespaces to internet
Use predictable JWT secret allowing MITM on Engine API
Disable critical security features (e.g., --insecure flag if exists)
Exfiltrate validator keys during initial setup
mitigations: Official Geth releases GPG signed by Ethereum Foundation
Checksums published on geth.ethereum.org for verification
Reproducible builds documented (though rarely independently verified)
Docker images published to ghcr.io/ethereum/client-go (GitHub container registry)
Configuration validation warnings in Geth startup logs
IaC (Terraform/Ansible) reduces configuration drift

actors.name: Ethereum Foundation / Core Developers
actors.description: Core protocol developers who maintain Geth codebase, define consensus rules via EIPs, and release new versions

operational_scenarios.description: Core devs implement EIPs per community consensus, maintain backward compatibility, and fix security bugs
trust_implications: Node operators trust that Geth implements Ethereum protocol correctly
Trust that security patches address real vulnerabilities without introducing backdoors
Trust that fork activation logic (e.g., Dencun at timestamp 1710338135) matches network consensus
Open source code auditable by community
operational_scenarios.deployment_pattern: Normal protocol evolution

operational_scenarios.description: Attacker compromises core dev GitHub account or GPG key to merge malicious code
trust_implications: Malicious code in release could steal keys, manipulate consensus, or create backdoor
Multi-party code review process should catch obvious attacks
Subtle bugs could be introduced that appear benign
GPG key compromise allows signing of malicious binaries
operational_scenarios.deployment_pattern: Supply chain attack at protocol level

operational_scenarios.description: Community disagrees on EIP (e.g., ProgPoW), Geth implements one side causing potential chain split
trust_implications: Node operators must choose which fork to follow
If contentious, could lead to replay attacks or network partition
Historical precedent: Ethereum/Ethereum Classic split after DAO fork
Geth's decision effectively determines 'canonical' chain due to market dominance
operational_scenarios.deployment_pattern: Governance crisis scenario (rare)

actors.trust_level_rationale: Node operators MUST trust that Geth codebase correctly implements Ethereum consensus rules. Open source allows verification but few operators audit code.
capabilities_if_honest: Implement EIPs as agreed by community via EIP process
Fix security vulnerabilities and issue timely patches
Maintain backward compatibility across upgrades
Provide migration paths for breaking changes (e.g., PoW to PoS)
Document configuration options and security best practices
capabilities_if_malicious: Introduce consensus bugs causing network splits
Embed backdoors in codebase (requires bypassing PR review)
Manipulate fork activation logic to favor specific actors
Sign compromised release binaries with stolen GPG key
Withhold security patches to exploit vulnerabilities
CANNOT force node operators to upgrade (operators control deployment)
mitigations: Open source code on GitHub (ethereum/go-ethereum) allows public audit
Multi-party PR review process requires approval from multiple maintainers
GPG signing of releases by known Ethereum Foundation keys
Community consensus required for contentious EIPs (rough consensus in ACD calls)
Alternative implementations (Besu, Nethermind, Erigon) provide diversity
Node operators free to fork codebase or delay upgrades if suspicious

components.name: Engine API (eth/catalyst)
components.description: Authenticated JSON-RPC interface for consensus layer to execution layer communication, implementing engine_newPayload, engine_forkchoiceUpdated, and engine_getPayload methods
components.trust_boundary: Trusted boundary - requires JWT authentication to prevent unauthorized payload submission or fork choice manipulation
trust_implications: AUTHENTICATED by JWT secret shared between Geth and CL at startup
Exposed only on localhost by default (--authrpc.addr=localhost:8551)
Compromise of JWT secret allows attacker to impersonate CL and inject invalid payloads
Invalid payloads rejected after validation but cause DoS overhead
validated_inputs: JWT token in Authorization header (HS256 signature)
Payload version matches fork (V1=Paris, V2=Shanghai, V3=Cancun, V4=Prague)
Block hash matches recomputed hash of header fields
Blob versioned hashes match transaction blob commitments
All standard block validation (state root, receipts root, gas used, etc.)
components.threat_model: TRUSTED interface assumed honest if authenticated. Malicious CL can DoS Geth but cannot force invalid state acceptance.

components.name: JSON-RPC Server (node/rpc)
components.description: Public/private RPC endpoint exposing Ethereum APIs (eth, net, web3, admin, debug, personal) over HTTP, WebSocket, and IPC transports
components.trust_boundary: Untrusted boundary for HTTP/WS - assumes adversarial clients. Trusted for IPC (local only).
trust_implications: HTTP/WebSocket: UNTRUSTED, must validate all inputs and enforce rate limits
IPC: TRUSTED (local socket, restricted file permissions)
Namespace-based access control: admin/debug/personal require explicit configuration
Default whitelist: only eth, net, web3 on HTTP to minimize attack surface
validated_inputs: JSON-RPC 2.0 message format validation
Batch request limits (--rpc.batch.limit, --rpc.batch.responsemaxsize)
Gas cap on eth_call to prevent DoS (--rpc.gascap, default 50M)
Query limits on eth_getLogs to prevent memory exhaustion (--rpc.logquerylimit, default 10000)
Execution timeout on expensive operations (--rpc.evmtimeout, default 5s)
components.threat_model: UNTRUSTED clients assumed malicious. Read-only namespaces safe. Admin/debug namespaces enable node compromise if exposed to attackers.

components.name: P2P Network Layer (p2p, eth/protocols/eth)
components.description: Peer-to-peer networking stack implementing devp2p RLPx protocol and ETH/68-69 subprotocol for block and transaction propagation
components.trust_boundary: Untrusted boundary - all P2P peers assumed adversarial
trust_implications: ALL received data validated before processing (blocks, transactions, headers)
Peer reputation tracking identifies and blacklists misbehaving peers
Connection limits prevent Sybil attacks exhausting resources
Fork ID prevents pollution from wrong network (mainnet vs testnet)
validated_inputs: RLPx protocol handshake with ECDH key exchange
Fork ID validation (Genesis hash + fork blocks/timestamps)
Message size limits (10MB max per ETH protocol)
Block validation via BlockValidator before chain incorporation
Transaction validation via TxPool before mempool admission
components.threat_model: UNTRUSTED network assumed hostile. Byzantine peers can cause DoS via resource exhaustion but cannot compromise safety (invalid data rejected).

components.name: Transaction Pool (core/txpool)
components.description: In-memory pool of pending and queued transactions awaiting block inclusion, with separate subpools for legacy (LegacyPool) and blob (BlobPool) transactions
components.trust_boundary: Untrusted boundary - assumes malicious transaction submissions
trust_implications: Stateless validation: signature, type, size, intrinsic gas, blob commitments
Stateful validation: nonce, balance, gas price vs base fee, blob base fee
Pool size limits prevent memory exhaustion (4096 pending, 1024 queued per account)
Eviction policy: lowest fee transactions dropped when pool full
validated_inputs: ECDSA signature verification (secp256k1) with address recovery
EIP-155 replay protection via chainID in signature
Nonce continuity (pending = next nonce, queued = future nonce)
Balance check: sender has value + gasLimit * gasFeeCap
Blob KZG commitment verification via point evaluation precompile (0x0a)
Transaction size under limit (128KB legacy, 256KB blob pool)
components.threat_model: UNTRUSTED submitters. All transactions validated before admission. Economic incentives (gas fees) deter spam. Invalid transactions rejected immediately.

components.name: Block Validator (core/block_validator)
components.description: Validates received blocks against consensus rules via ValidateBody (structural) and ValidateState (execution) checks before chain incorporation
components.trust_boundary: Trust enforcement - prevents invalid blocks from entering canonical chain
trust_implications: CRITICAL SAFETY COMPONENT: last line of defense against invalid state
Validates ALL blocks regardless of source (P2P, Engine API, local mining)
Consensus bug in validator = network-wide vulnerability
Performance critical: must validate blocks within 12-second slot time
validated_inputs: Block structure: transaction count, uncle count, withdrawals (post-Shanghai)
Merkle roots: transaction root, uncle root, withdrawals root, receipts root
Gas accounting: gas used, gas limit, base fee calculation (EIP-1559)
Blob accounting: blob gas used, excess blob gas (EIP-4844)
State root: matches after executing all transactions
Execution requests root: deposits, withdrawals, consolidations (Prague+)
components.threat_model: Defends against BYZANTINE BLOCKS from any source. Must be deterministic and bug-free to prevent consensus splits.

components.name: EVM (core/vm)
components.description: Ethereum Virtual Machine implementing all opcodes, precompiled contracts, and gas metering for transaction execution
components.trust_boundary: Trust enforcement - executes untrusted bytecode in sandboxed environment
trust_implications: CRITICAL SAFETY COMPONENT: must enforce gas limits to prevent infinite loops
Executes untrusted bytecode from contracts and EOAs
Gas metering prevents DoS via expensive operations
Precompiled contracts implement cryptography deterministically (ECRECOVER, SHA256, KZG, BLS)
validated_inputs: Gas limit enforced per opcode (out of gas = revert)
Stack depth limit (1024) prevents unbounded recursion
Memory expansion cost quadratic to prevent DoS
Access lists (EIP-2929) reduce storage access cost after first touch
Precompiled contract input validation (e.g., BLS point validity)
components.threat_model: Executes UNTRUSTED CODE in sandboxed environment. Gas metering ensures termination. Must be deterministic to prevent consensus splits.

components.name: State Database (core/state, triedb)
components.description: Merkle Patricia Trie database storing world state (accounts, storage, code) with cryptographic commitment via state root
components.trust_boundary: Trusted persistence - assumes disk integrity, but validates all state transitions
trust_implications: State root binds all account balances, nonces, storage, code hashes
Corrupted disk data detected by state root mismatch during block validation
Pruning retains last 128 blocks in memory (TriesInMemory) for reorg support
PBSS (Path-Based State Scheme) enables efficient state access vs legacy hash-based scheme
validated_inputs: All state transitions via EVM execution validated by block validator
State root recomputed after every block and checked against header
Trie nodes authenticated by Merkle proofs
Snapshot layer provides fast state access with fallback to trie
components.threat_model: Trusted storage layer but defended by cryptographic commitments. Disk corruption or tampering detected by state root mismatch.

components.name: Keystore (accounts/keystore)
components.description: Encrypted storage for private keys using Web3 Secret Storage Definition (scrypt KDF), managed locally by Geth or externally by Clef
components.trust_boundary: Trusted key material - compromise of keystore or passphrase = theft of funds
trust_implications: CRITICAL SECURITY COMPONENT: stores private keys for validator signing
Passphrase-based encryption via scrypt KDF with configurable work factor
Weak passphrase vulnerable to brute force (scrypt slows but doesn't prevent)
File permissions critical: keystore files should be 0600 (owner read/write only)
Clef alternative isolates keys from Geth process
validated_inputs: Passphrase provided by operator at unlock time
Scrypt work factor validation (N, r, p parameters)
Private key validity (secp256k1 curve point)
Address derivation matches key (keccak256(pubkey)[12:])
components.threat_model: TRUSTED by operator but HIGH-VALUE TARGET for attackers. Compromise = complete key theft. Encrypted at rest but plaintext in memory when unlocked.

components.name: Miner/Builder (miner/worker)
components.description: Block construction engine that selects transactions from pool, executes them, and assembles payload for consensus layer proposal
components.trust_boundary: Trusted block production - operator controls which transactions included (censorship risk)
trust_implications: Transaction selection controlled by operator: can censor or prioritize specific transactions
MEV extraction: operator can reorder transactions for profit (front-running, sandwiching)
Payload must pass validation by own node before submission to CL
External builder (MEV-Boost) outsources this function to third party
validated_inputs: Payload attributes from CL (timestamp, feeRecipient, withdrawals, beaconRoot)
Transactions from pool sorted by effective priority fee
System calls executed before transactions (beacon root, parent hash, withdrawals)
Block size limit enforced (EIP-7934: 8MB max minus 1MB buffer)
Blob limit enforced (Cancun: 6 blobs, configurable in later forks)
components.threat_model: TRUSTED by operator for liveness and MEV revenue. Operator can censor but all produced blocks validated locally before submission.

components.name: Downloader / Sync (eth/downloader)
components.description: Fetches historical blocks and state from P2P peers to catch up with canonical chain head, supporting snap sync (state), full sync (all blocks), and archive mode
components.trust_boundary: Untrusted P2P data - validates all received data before incorporation
trust_implications: Snap sync downloads state snapshot from peers (faster but trusts state root)
Full sync validates every block from genesis (slow but fully trustless)
Archive mode retains all historical state (high disk usage)
Checkpoint sync trusts finalized checkpoint to skip initial sync
validated_inputs: All received blocks validated via BlockValidator
State snapshot authenticated via state root in finalized checkpoint
Peer-provided data cross-checked against multiple peers
Bad blocks tracked ephemerally to avoid re-processing
components.threat_model: UNTRUSTED P2P network. Snap sync trades trust for speed (trusts finalized state root). Full sync fully trustless. Eclipse attack can feed wrong chain.

components.name: ChainConfig (params/config.go)
components.description: Hardcoded and operator-configured fork activation parameters (block numbers and timestamps) defining when consensus rule changes activate
components.trust_boundary: TRUSTED configuration - incorrect values cause chain split from network
trust_implications: CRITICAL CONFIGURATION: wrong fork activation = consensus split
Mainnet values hardcoded in params/config.go (London: 12965000, Paris: TTD 58750e18, etc.)
Override flags (--override.osaka, --override.verkle) allow testing on custom networks
Node operator trusts that Geth's default config matches community consensus
validated_inputs: Fork timestamps must be monotonically increasing
Genesis config loaded from file or defaults
Override flags validated for sane values
Fork detector warns if chain config doesn't match connected peers
components.threat_model: TRUSTED by operator but CRITICAL for consensus. Misconfiguration or malicious override causes network split. Geth defaults assumed correct for mainnet.

components.name: Precompiled Contracts (core/vm/contracts.go)
components.description: Native implementations of cryptographic operations at addresses 0x01-0x11 (ECRECOVER, SHA256, BLAKE2F, KZG, BLS12-381) with fixed gas costs
components.trust_boundary: Trust enforcement - must be deterministic and bug-free for consensus
trust_implications: CRITICAL CONSENSUS COMPONENT: bugs cause network splits
Cryptographic implementations must match spec exactly (bit-for-bit)
Gas costs must be deterministic and sufficient to prevent DoS
KZG and BLS12-381 rely on trusted setup ceremony parameters
validated_inputs: Input length validation per precompile spec
Point validity checks for BLS12-381 curve operations
KZG commitment/proof format validation
Gas cost calculation before execution (insufficient gas = failure)
components.threat_model: TRUSTED implementations assumed correct. Bugs in precompiles (especially KZG, BLS) could break L2 data availability or future Verkle proofs.

trust_boundaries.enforced_by: JWT authentication (HS256 signature), localhost-only binding by default
trust_boundaries.threat: Unauthenticated attacker impersonating CL to inject malicious payloads
trust_boundaries.mitigation: JWT secret shared securely, payload validation rejects invalid blocks

trust_boundaries.enforced_by: Namespace whitelisting (eth/net/web3 only by default), rate limits, gas caps
trust_boundaries.threat: Malicious client exploiting admin/debug APIs or DoS via expensive queries
trust_boundaries.mitigation: Admin/debug require explicit --http.api, query limits enforced

trust_boundaries.enforced_by: Full validation of all received data (blocks, transactions), peer reputation
trust_boundaries.threat: Byzantine peers sending invalid blocks/txs to corrupt state or DoS node
trust_boundaries.mitigation: BlockValidator and TxPool validation reject invalid data, peer blacklisting

trust_boundaries.threat: Attacker stealing keystore files and brute-forcing passphrase
trust_boundaries.mitigation: Strong passphrase required, scrypt slows brute force, Clef isolates keys

trust_boundaries.enforced_by: Signature verification, nonce/balance checks, gas validation, KZG proofs
trust_boundaries.threat: Malicious user submitting invalid or replay transactions
trust_boundaries.mitigation: Comprehensive validation before mempool admission, EIP-155 replay protection

key_trust_assumptions: Consensus Client trusted for liveness (providing fork choice), not safety (Geth validates all payloads)
Node Operator and Deployer fully trusted - have root access to keys and configuration
P2P Network and RPC Clients assumed adversarial - all inputs validated
Core Developers trusted to implement protocol correctly - open source allows audit
Cryptographic primitives (ECDSA, KZG, BLS, keccak256) assumed secure
Precompiled contracts deterministic and correct - bugs cause consensus splits
State Database integrity protected by state root - disk corruption detectable
critical_security_boundaries: Engine API: JWT authentication prevents unauthorized CL impersonation
Block Validator: Last line of defense against invalid state, must be bug-free
TxPool Validator: Prevents invalid transactions from entering mempool
EVM Gas Metering: Ensures execution termination, prevents DoS
Keystore Encryption: Protects private keys with passphrase, weak passphrase = key theft
operational_trade_offs: MEV-Boost: Outsources block building for higher revenue but adds liveness dependency and censorship risk
Snap Sync: Faster sync but trusts finalized state root (vs full sync from genesis)
Clef: Isolates keys from Geth but adds complexity and potential misconfiguration
Public RPC: Provides service to users but exposes attack surface (mitigated by namespace whitelisting)
P2P: Decentralized but vulnerable to eclipse attacks if attacker controls routing
unclear_areas: UNCLEAR: Operational model for MEV relays (centralized Flashbots vs permissionless relay network) - not specified in Geth codebase, external dependency
UNCLEAR: How node operators verify Geth binary integrity in practice - GPG signature verification documented but adoption rate unknown
UNCLEAR: Incident response process if consensus bug discovered - no formal protocol in codebase, relies on social coordination
UNCLEAR: Long-term incentive alignment for core developers - funded by Ethereum Foundation but no explicit governance over codebase direction
notes: Geth is the dominant Ethereum execution client (~80% market share as of 2024), making it a critical single point of failure for network
Post-Merge architecture splits trust: Consensus Layer (Prysm/Lighthouse) handles fork choice, Execution Layer (Geth) validates all payloads
MEV supply chain adds external actors (builders, relays) not in Geth codebase but operationally critical for >90% of validators
Trust model heavily relies on cryptographic assumptions: ECDSA for transaction signatures, KZG for blob commitments, BLS for consensus (via CL)
Operational security depends on node operator competence: weak RPC config or keystore passphrase undermines protocol-level security
